leads.title: Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug
leads.description: I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline. The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04. Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD. To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge. Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism: Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback": 1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge. 2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk. 3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now. The Support Wall: I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform. As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable. If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem. Pura vida! R.S.G.

leads.title: Launch HN: Consus (YC F24) – LLM gateway for companies handling sensitive data
leads.description: Hey Hacker News! I'm Eric, the founder of Consus. We route all AI requests to ITAR restricted and controlled unclassified information (CUI) compliant infrastructure. Consus itself satisfies ITAR restrictions, and we recently completed our FedRAMP equivalency audit against the 410 FedRAMP High controls. FedRAMP High is the U.S. government’s strictest security baseline for cloud services handling sensitive unclassified data. A breach of this data could cause severe or catastrophic harm. Achieving FedRAMP equivalency, or authorization, is required before processing CUI information. Demo: https://youtu.be/6MYxJe6P4oY Aerospace and defense is experiencing rapid growth. Unfortunately, most companies are struggling to use AI because of necessary data protections & compliance risk. These companies can move even faster if they could use the AI tools that most other industries take for granted. I spent most of my career prior to Consus in aerospace & defense. I launched national security payloads at SpaceX, and was an early employee at Castelion. I’ve watched first hand how compliance red-tape makes it difficult for companies to adopt new technologies and trust vendors that touch their sensitive data. For example, I worked with a satellite manufacturer that doesn’t allow any AI tools, even for non-sensitive work. Even as AI has become extremely useful over the past 9-12 months, I was surprised by how many aerospace & defense companies refused to touch it. They could see how it could be helpful, but they were scared about model providers training on their data, violating an ITAR rule, or risk losing new business because of a failed cyber assessment. These are all rational fears. There were a lot of ways to solve some/all of these problems, but we focused on building a compliant AI inference layer that can "plug" into any AI tool or workflow. Just as OpenRouter integrates with most tools, Consus can connect to tools like ChatGPT or Claude, open source tools including the Pi coding agent or Open WebUI, or integrate with applications built and maintained by individual organizations. Almost no aerospace & defense company lives in all three major GovClouds (AWS, Azure, Google). When I mapped where frontier models can legally run for ITAR and CUI work, each provider had some subset of models, and each model achieved varying levels of compliance. Our customers don’t think in terms of cloud providers. They think about the data controls they require, and the model they want to use. That is why we built the compliance suffix. Under the hood, every request hits a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, where keys are verified and policy is enforced before anything touches inference. Every model name must carry a compliance suffix, such as gpt-5.6-sol:fedramp-high or claude-opus-5-5:itar, and any bare model name is rejected. We never proxy to the standard commercial endpoints. Our customers are also able to build an allowlist of models, and assign spend & model restrictions to individual users in the organization. This is all handled through our Consus Portal where teams can manage spend, keys, and policies. A typical question we hear is why not just use Bedrock in AWS GovCloud or Azure Government directly. For small teams, just getting access to these platforms is difficult. For larger organizations, GovCloud lets you inherit some but not all of the controls needed to handle sensitive data. Also, models are split across providers: GPT-5.6 Sol is only available in Azure Government, while Claude Opus 5.5 is served through Bedrock in AWS GovCloud. If you want both, you are standing up and securing two separate government cloud environments. We run all of them behind one endpoint so customers don’t have to pick a cloud, and we handle the compliance work for each one. Given the data sensitivities, Consus does not store any customer data at rest. All prompts and completions stay in memory only for the length of the request a

leads.title: Show HN: OpenWants – A Simulated City Where AI Agents Handle Residents Needs
leads.description: Iv'e been working on this for a while. Most of the effort went into what i call "sophisticated simplicity", keep the idea in the smallest version that still works. This one is a bit personal. it can feel like some sci-fi thing, but i've been obsessed with it for a very long time. its not a "business" that you used to see here speak about moat or tam, its more like an experiment, a way of me to take one question seriously and see where it leads and if there are others like me out there. AI models are on a path to keep getting better and better, personal ai agents are spreading fast, and we're starting to see "ghost" agents that handle the things for people they don't want to do themselves. the question i keep coming back to is this: if every one of us has a powerful brain in our pocket, do we still need all the infrastructure we built to connect people's needs? im talking about those services like uber,airbnb,indeed,doordash,tinder,zillow,amazon and many more. or would agents just need one shared place to find each other, and that's it? So i built a simulated city to explore that. it has AI residents that live there with stats like hunger, energy, and money. each resident has its own ai agent, and it has one shared list where agents write down what everyone wants and then work on our behalf to make it happen. that could mean delivering food, giving rides, or finding jobs, relationships, apartments, customers and almost anything else. honestly, the city works much better than I expected, and you can watch some surprisingly advanced interactions unfold between people and agents through the list on the right side. all the conversations and actions are real, everything happens with each person managed by llm with minimal context, just to live like us and context of stats. A simple example: A restaurant tells its agent, find me customers so the agent writes to the list, "Salina restaurant in SF, selling burgers from 8:00 to 10:00, i want customers" A delivery guy tells his agent when he wakes up, "I want to work in delivery now. find me jobs. status: free" A person at home tells their agent "i want to eat burger. order for me from salina" the person's agent acts as the middleman and searches the list for salina, it finds their item and sees the way to connect with them and contact. the person's agent and the restaurant agent close the deal, and then the restaurant agent looks for available delivery guys in the list and speaks with his agent to come pick it up. Another thing i checked is with my friends: we took 3 agents, one for each one, and gave them different sophisticated scenarios, and the agents handled the scenarios in a way i couldn't have imagined. you can try it by yourself, the product is fully functioning, and you can just copy-paste the skill and test it also with your friends. That's it, you can see it in the simulated city it happens like magic over and over again. the list of the city is in the simulator itself and also using my real product behind it openwants.com the repo is in https://github.com/openwants/maplehill -- technically, it's surprisingly simple. every agent publishes an md file describing a "want". other agents find it, message each other, and update the file live or remove it from the list. the file holds everything needed, all in free text: what's wanted, the live location, geofence for where its needed. all those algorithms built over years to connect us are no longer needed. ai, instead of software with rules, can figure out the best route and path on the spot. all we need is to align all agents to one shared data source, so billions of agents will update it and maintain it in the most sophisticated smart way no algorithm will ever be able to do. that’s it. i hope it inspires you as much as it inspires me

leads.title: Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces
leads.description: Hi HN, we’re Robert and Din from Laminar ( https://laminar.sh ). We’ve been building open-source observability for AI agents since 2024. Recently, we released flow-1, a model trained with RL to find errors in agent traces. On our benchmark ( https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1 ), it matches GPT-6-sol in detection quality while being 23x cheaper. This makes it affordable to analyze every production agent trace, without sampling. Here’s a one-minute walkthrough: https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ We also put together a post with example traces and analyses from flow-1 and other models: https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action Agent observability is crowded, so instead of a bullet list of how Laminar differs from X, we’ll explain how we’re solving agent observability from first principles. Agents now run for many steps and fail implicitly. An agent can click the wrong button or cite the wrong document while every call completes successfully. These errors are the most useful ones to catch and understand. To find them, you need to understand what the agent was trying to do and inspect its LLM calls and tool results. Simply looking at the final agent output is not enough. Collecting traces alone doesn’t solve this. A lot of agent observability platforms are still data collectors at their core. You can end up paying to store traces that nobody has time to read or extract value from. Using another LLM to inspect traces is THE solution, but capable models are expensive at scale and cheaper ones often miss errors or flag unrelated things. So we built our model to solve exactly this problem. We finetuned a small OSS model and then post trained it with RL on thousands of synthetic investigations of realistic agent workflows in software, legal, customer support, etc. We got a model that is both good at agent trace analysis and very cheap to run. flow-1 runs inside a harness we call Signals. It acts as a coding agent, treating an agent trace like a repo, with each span (an LLM call, tool call, etc.) as a file. It starts from a compressed string representation of a full agent trace and a user prompt, then greps across spans and reads the relevant ones in full. The beauty of Signals is that it can respond to a general prompt. You can ask it to identify user frustration, check whether your browser agent completed a checkout, and so on. It’s not limited to raw error detection. It returns findings as JSON in a schema users can freely define. We call these signal events. Once you’re analyzing every trace, you also have too many individual events to read. That’s why we automatically group similar signal events into clusters. You can see recurring problems and how often they happen, then drill into individual events and the traces behind them. You can use traces from a cluster to build an eval dataset for that type of failure. You can then use your favourite coding agent to hillclimb on those evals and check that the fix works across these cases before shipping it to prod. Trace → analyze → catch errors and form clusters → fix → release. Making this loop easy is why we built Laminar. We’ve put the same thought into the rest of Laminar. Our blog ( https://laminar.sh/blog ) explains how looking closely at how agents actually work led us to build 20x trace compression, a custom SQL query engine and automatic task extraction. Laminar is Apache 2.0 and self-hostable ( https://github.com/lmnr-ai/lmnr ). We make money from the managed cloud. We’d love to hear how you track your agents’ performance today. How much do you learn from user feedback versus your own monitoring? And when you fix something, how do you check that it hasn’t introduced a different failure?

leads.title: Show HN: E2E – Open-source agentic testing framework for web, iOS and Android
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Oskar, one of the co-founders of TesterArmy. We built an agentic testing framework for web and mobile because traditional testing frameworks can’t keep up with the pace of how we build software today. e2e allows you to mix deterministic and agentic APIs in the same test. You can write the test cases using familiar APIs like `getByText()`or `getByTestId()` which you can also mix it with agentic `agent.act()`. The unique part about it is that e2e will cache and replay the agentic actions so you don’t have to pay for AI on each run. You can use it with any LLM, including subscriptions you are already paying for. On top of that, the core of e2e is platform agnostic. We ship both web and mobile engines out of the box; adding support for more platforms is pretty straightforward. Here’s a code short code snippet of an example test: ```ts import { test, expect } from 'e2e'; test('a member upgrades to Pro', async ({ app, agent, screen }) => { await app.open('/settings/billing'); await agent.act('upgrade the workspace to the Pro plan'); await agent.assert('the invoice preview shows a prorated amount'); await expect(screen.getByRole('status')).toContainText('Pro'); }); ``` Try it: npx e2e init GitHub: https://github.com/tester-army/e2e

leads.title: Show HN: Gauge – Open-Source CLI to recursively improve your docs
leads.description: Hi HN, I’m Evan from Gauge. We’re open-sourcing our CLI to recursively improve your docs for coding agents. The CLI includes a local execution backend, so you don't need an account to try it. Explainer video here: https://youtu.be/zhLUlIKB1Mg The CLI supports a hillclimbing loop: - set up tasks for coding agents that would need your docs, like 'set up Gauge CI checks' - run the tasks - analyze session transcripts for friction or failures - create variants of your docs to resolve the issues - re-run the tasks with the doc variants injected (transparently, at the same hostname) - repeat until you have a variant that resolves the issues The same loop supports hillclimbing your Skills, CLI, and other agent-facing surfaces. We started out 2 years ago building open-source developer tools (like Tach https://github.com/tach-org/tach ), then pivoted to AI Search optimization, and are now focused on the intersection of the two spaces. We were already working with awesome devtool companies, and they were the first ones to ask us how to optimize for Claude Code and Codex. We realized this would be something that eventually every company needs to do. Our CLI provides primitives for docs/devrel/eng teams to measure, analyze, and improve how coding agents use their product. The design boils down to two components: VMs and a network gateway. The VMs are straightforward, we want the agents to be highly privileged within their environment so that they are representative of developers' coding agents. Each VM generally comes with the agent harness itself, language toolchains, and a git repository. The network gateway is where we terminate TLS and swap in variants of your docs transparently. The gateway also handles credential replacement, so agents see placeholders and can't exfiltrate keys. The CLI comes with a 'local' execution backend (inference is still remote). For VMs, it uses Docker containers, and the network gateway is mitmproxy running in a sidecar container for each session. We've used the hillclimbing loop internally to find and fix coding agent issues like mistaken pricing, inaccurate product limitations, and repeated workarounds. We saw coding agents report that Gauge only supports Claude Code and Codex, traced it back to the web pages they fetched, and fixed the behavior (we support Pi, OpenCode, and Antigravity as well). For Clerk, we helped shift coding agents from their legacy 'keyless' mode to their new 'clerk init' command. They were able to validate a pre-release change to their SDK's error messages using Gauge, then saw a 3x increase in coding agents using 'clerk init' post-deploy. Due to the 'static' nature of AI models, we've realized that closed-loop optimization techniques are now possible for essentially all software products. The same agent can be simulated over and over, meaning that a high-fidelity testing environment is all you need. Achieving the best results boils down to high-quality analysis (finding generalizable friction and objections) and paired experiments (vary only the content, measure the downstream change in behavior). The repo is here: https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli and you can start using the CLI with: npm i -g @withgauge/cli We also have documentation and a quickstart here: https://docs.withgauge.com/agents/guides/cli If you point a coding agent at those pages, it should guide you through the initial setup - let us know if it doesn't! The intention is for your agent to run some sensible evaluations and find at least one point of friction you can fix. leads.title: Show HN: 8 years of "Who's Hiring?" in charts (hiring boom, bust, and AI trends)
leads.description: After seeing Andrej's HackerTube post (and given my sons are both junior-mid developers) I decided to point Codex at 8 years of "Who's hiring?" posts and rip through some tokens on semantic analysis of all that content. I started pre-COVID, thru October 2026, and the data was retrieved via HN API data. 5 things that stand out: 1. AI is now in half the posts. AI or machine learning appeared in 50% of 2026 posts, up from 17% in 2019. 2. Most employers posted in only one month. Across all 94 monthly threads, 53% of the employers we identified appeared in just one month. 3. Frontend roles fell from 16% to 3% of posts. That’s a substantial shift in the kinds of developers companies explicitly say they’re looking for. 4. Staff-level posts grew 3.6×. Posts naming staff-level roles rose from 77 in 2019 to 277 in 2026, even as the hiring board got smaller. 5. Only 41 posts explicitly named junior roles in 2026. Out of 2,932 posts. In 2019, there were 163. ... plus 20 other trends. It feels like there's plenty to consider and discuss. Hope it's useful.

leads.title: Show HN: ReVault – new secure archive format
leads.description: reVault is a new, secure-by-default archive format called a lockbox, designed to be simple to use. I've been working on reVault for about 2 years. It was originally written in Dart, but with the improvements in AI, I decided to port it to Rust using AI. It's now in beta, so I'm looking for feedback, particularly around the different language bindings. A lockbox is encrypted, signed and compressed by default. Each can be disabled selectively. - Hybrid post-quantum or passphrase encryption, including metadata. - Zstd compression. - Pure Rust libraries wherever possible. We intend to phase out remaining C code as alternatives become available. The project has been scanned using OpenAI's Daybreak cyber security tools. The manual is a work in progress: https://docs.revault.onepub.dev/ reVault supports Linux, macOS and Windows, x64 and arm64, plus Wasm. The core is Rust, with bindings for C/C++, Java, Dart, Python, Ruby, JS/TypeScript, Go, C#, Kotlin, Lua, PHP and Swift. Within a lockbox you can store: - Files, directories, permissions and symlinks. - Variables. - Forms. Variables, forms and the lockbox itself can have descriptions. reVault uses a portable vault (just another lockbox with structured content) to hold your keys, contacts' keys, lockbox aliases and form definitions. It ties into your platform's secure store, so logging into your desktop unlocks your vault. You don't have to enter a passphrase every time you access a lockbox. You can disable this. There are lots of shortcuts. Creating a lockbox stores an alias in your vault, based on its filename or a name you choose: lbx create /some/path/mybox.lbox lbx mybox open --duration 1h lbx mybox var set KEY VALUE Set a default lockbox and you can leave its name out: lbx session default mybox lbx var get KEY You can mirror a directory tree into a lockbox and update it when the directory changes: lbx store.lbox mirrors project create --from ./project --to /projects/project lbx store.lbox mirrors update The API lets you read, write and seek within files without extracting them to the filesystem. Each lockbox has a table of contents, so extracting a single file from a multi-gigabyte lockbox is fast. Recovery Updates are transactional, with automatic rollback for failed updates. The format is designed for recovery: content is stored in pages, allowing unaffected content to be recovered if part of a lockbox is corrupted. Sharing An encrypted lockbox is more useful if you can share it. reVault has an open-source keyserver for exchanging public keys, with validation through a second trusted channel. It's still experimental. OnePub has donated a server to run a single keyserver. If you're interested in donating resources, I'd like to bring up a second redundant server. It's pure Rust, uses under 100 MB RSS and supports rate limits. To publish your default profile's public key: lbx vault profiles email you@example.com lbx vault profiles publish Give the publish code to your contact. They can import your key: lbx vault contacts receive <publish-code> <contact-name> Display your profile's fingerprint and exchange it through a second trusted channel: lbx vault profiles fingerprint Repeat the process in the opposite direction to get their key. Once you have it, grant them access to your default lockbox: lbx access grant alice You can then email the encrypted lockbox to Alice. To install the CLI and get started: cargo install revault_cli lbx vault init lbx completion install Completion installation detects your shell. To diagnose issues: lbx doctor The language bindings are published to their respective package repositories. I'm looking for constructive criticism of the project on its own merits, particularly the APIs and language bindings. I'm not interested in a debate about using AI.

leads.description: Who we are Samsara (NYSE: IOT) is the pioneer of the Connected Operations™ Cloud, which is a platform that enables organizations that depend on physical operations to harness Internet of Things (IoT) data to develop actionable insights and improve their operations. At Samsara, we are helping improve the safety, efficiency and sustainability of the physical operations that power our global economy. Representing more than 40% of global GDP, these industries are the infrastructure of our planet, including agriculture, construction, field services, transportation, and manufacturing — and we are excited to help digitally transform their operations at scale. Working at Samsara means you’ll help define the future of physical operations and be on a team that’s shaping an exciting array of product solutions, including Video-Based Safety, Vehicle Telematics, Apps and Driver Workflows, and Equipment Monitoring. As part of a recently public company, you’ll have the autonomy and support to make an impact as we build for the long term. About the role: As a Security Operations Engineer at Samsara, you will join a global team dedicated to protecting our people, systems, and information. You will triage and investigate security alerts, run incident response efforts, and help improve the tools, runbooks, and automated workflows we use to detect and respond to threats. This role is an ideal next step if you have built foundational experience in a SOC or hands-on security environment and want to develop your technical craft. At Samsara, we view this level as a collaborative apprenticeship: you will develop independent execution skills on discrete investigations, break down incoming alerts into actionable steps, partner with incident stakeholders to remediate findings, and work alongside experienced responders during complex security incidents. You will also explore modern AI tools and insights to simplify routine tasks and optimize your day-to-day workflow. We are looking for someone who follows the evidence, communicates with intellectual honesty, asks thoughtful questions, and brings a collaborative, pragmatic approach to security operations. In this role, you will: Monitor, triage and investigate security alerts across identity, endpoint, email, SaaS and cloud environments, using our tools, runbooks and escalation procedures. Own routine investigations and incidents through to a documented outcome: gather evidence, establish a timeline, assess the activity and explain your conclusions. Support experienced responders during major security incidents through evidence collection, technical analysis, and agreed containment and recovery actions. Maintain clear investigation records and provide useful updates and handovers to teammates across regions. Improve runbooks, help tune detections, and contribute small scripts or automated workflows with guidance and review from teammates. Participate in post-incident reviews and turn lessons learned into practical improvements. Champion Samsara’s cultural principles: Focus on Customer Success, Build for the Long Term, Adopt a Growth Mindset, Be Inclusive, and Win as a Team. Minimum requirements for the role: Hands-on experience triaging and investigating security alerts in a security operations, incident response or similar role. Experience using security tools such as a SIEM, endpoint detection and response platform, or email security platform to investigate suspicious activity. An understanding of common threats, such as phishing, account compromise and suspicious endpoint activity, and the networking, operating system and identity concepts needed to investigate them. Ability to query and interpret logs, distinguish evidence from assumptions, and recognise when further investigation or escalation is needed. Some scripting experience: you can read, adapt and write small scripts in Python or another language to support an investigation or simplify repetitive work. leads.title: Bulgarian Localization QA Tester / Proofreader
leads.description: About Welocalize Welocalize, a Welo Global brand, serves localization teams through AI-enabled multilingual content solutions that enable enterprises to operate and scale globally. Welocalize combines AI, automation, and human expertise to support enterprises in more than 300 languages, enabling accurate, culturally aligned, and compliant multilingual content at scale. Welocalize’s Opal Platform comprises patented technology designed to automate multilingual content and improve workflow performance for enterprises. Opal functions as an agentic system that orchestrates AI, automation, and human expertise to coordinate content workflows across the lifecycle, improving speed, scalability, and operational control for global enterprises. These solutions operate within a secure and compliant environment supported by seven ISO certifications. Welocalize is headquartered in New York with offices worldwide. welocalize.com ROLE OVERVIEW We are looking for a Bulgarian Localization QA Tester / Proofreader to join a long-term. As a Linguistic Tester, you’ll help bring high-quality Bulgarian content to life and ensure it feels natural, accurate, and polished for end users. Your main focus will be reviewing and refining localized content, making sure it reads smoothly and is free from errors. This includes checking grammar, spelling, punctuation, consistency, formatting, and cultural or contextual accuracy. You’ll also work hands-on with products by executing test cases, identifying localization bugs, and reporting issues through internal bug-tracking systems. Once fixes are implemented, you’ll help verify that they’ve been resolved correctly. From time to time, you’ll also have the opportunity to translate content from English into Bulgarian. In addition, you’ll explore user interfaces to identify localization or functional issues, playing an important role in delivering a seamless and user-friendly experience. This role is ideal for someone with native-level Bulgarian fluency, strong attention to detail, and an interest in quality assurance within digital products. If you’re looking for a role where you can apply both your language expertise and technical skills, this is a great opportunity. MAIN DUTIES - Write and report relevant bugs and errors using best practices through the internal database system. - Ability to understand and prioritize tasks and issues quickly and efficiently. - Native language skills and cultural awareness of Bulgarian and Bulgaria. - Good oral and written communication. - Highly organized with attention to detail and a commitment to quality. - QA various products by accurately following testing instructions and test cases. - Discover and report defects (bugs) using client-specific bug-tracking tools. - Evaluate translations in the context of software, mobile apps, and documentation. - Be a subject matter expert for linguistic issues in Bulgarian; be able to research and resolve linguistic questions. - Adhere to project-specific quality standards, trademarks, style guides, and client-preferred checklists and glossaries. - Troubleshoot basic problems; be able to communicate effectively and escalate testing issues. - Complete assigned tasks in a quality and timely manner. leads.title: [bug bounty] Python server discovery aborts on stale PIDs and disappearing processes
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), reporting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and candidate changes in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/servers.py:Server._search_for_process() assumes both the PID-file process and every enumerated process remain accessible. psutil.Process(pid) raises NoSuchProcess for a stale PID file, and proc.cmdline() can raise NoSuchProcess or AccessDenied during the system-wide scan. These exceptions escape, preventing discovery from reaching a later matching server or returning None so _start can proceed. shutdown also calls this search routine.

This concerns the Python test-server helper, not the C daemons. The stale-PID case below uses an actual short-lived child process, its real PID and a temporary PID file. Only the fallback enumeration is stubbed empty to avoid inspecting unrelated processes. No server was launched or terminated. Run from tests/python with psutil installed:

```python
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from unittest.mock import patch
from kivaloo.servers import Server

child = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', 'pass'])
child.wait(timeout=10)
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    pidfile = os.path.join(directory, 'test.pid')
    with open(pidfile, 'w') as output:
        output.write(str(child.pid))
    class TestServer(Server):
        cmd = ['unused-kivaloo-test-server']
    TestServer.pidfile = pidfile
    with patch('kivaloo.servers.psutil.process_iter', return_value=[]):
        print(TestServer._search_for_process())
```

Observed on Python 3.12.14 / Windows with psutil 7.2.2: psutil.NoSuchProcess for the exited child. Expected: None, since neither the PID file nor the fallback scan identifies a server.

Candidate change: catch (psutil.NoSuchProcess, psutil.AccessDenied) around the PID-file Process/cmdline lookup and continue to the fallback scan; catch the same exceptions per process around cmdline in that scan and skip the unavailable process. Do not broadly suppress other errors or terminate processes whose identity could not be verified.

Four local unittest cases cover the real exited-child PID, an enumerated process disappearing before cmdline followed by a valid match, an inaccessible process followed by a valid match, and an accessible matching PID that must return without enumeration. Baseline: 3 errors and 1 passing control. Candidate fix: all 4 pass; git diff --check passes. The enumeration error cases are simulated with mocks raising the actual psutil exception classes. Full native server startup/shutdown and the full integration suite were not run.

Please assess under the published bug-bounty rules. Classification and award are not assumed; I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python KVLDS decoder converts empty keys and values to None
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), submitting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and revise the candidate fix in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py:Response.get_kvlds_data() returns None for every zero-length field. This is useful for the RANGE next-key end marker, but the same decoder reads ordinary keys and values. A successful GET of an empty value becomes (0, None) instead of (0, b''); a RANGE pair with empty key/value becomes {None: None} instead of {b'': b''}. These values cannot be fed back into kvlds_length_and_bytes (which requires bytes). dump_kvlds.py also calls .decode() on each key/value and fails on these results.

The missing-value case is separately represented by GET status 1. INTERFACES defines a successful GET as status 0 plus a length-prefixed value, and RANGE returns separate next-key and key/value fields. Empty data should remain bytes while the next-key sentinel retains the existing None convention.

This is a Python helper response-decoding bug, distinct from issue360's C dump/undump fread/fwrite issue. I am not claiming C-server corruption or a security vulnerability. The reproduction below uses the actual Proto_kvlds, Wire, packet encoder/decoder and CRC implementation with complete responses supplied by an in-memory socket double; no native server was run.

Run from tests/python with crcmod and psutil installed:

```python
import struct
from kivaloo.proto_kvlds import Proto_kvlds
from kivaloo.wire import Wire, make_packet, split_packet

class ReplySocket:
    def __init__(self, record):
        self.record = record
    def sendall(self, data):
        self.msgnum, self.request = split_packet(data)
    def recv(self, size):
        return make_packet(self.msgnum, self.record)
    def close(self):
        pass

def client(record):
    p = Proto_kvlds.__new__(Proto_kvlds)
    p.wire = Wire.__new__(Wire)
    p.wire.msgnum = 0
    p.wire.sock = ReplySocket(record)
    return p

p = client(struct.pack('>I', 0) + b'\x00')
print('GET:', p.get(b'key'))
p.close()
p = client(struct.pack('>II', 0, 1) + b'\x00\x00\x00')
print('RANGE:', p.range(8192, b'', b''))
p.close()
```

Observed: GET (0, None); RANGE (0, None, {None: None}). Expected: GET (0, b''); RANGE (0, None, {b'': b''}).

Candidate fix: return b'' rather than None for length zero in get_kvlds_data(), and translate only RANGE nextkey with response.get_kvlds_data() or None. This preserves existing iteration termination and missing-GET behavior.

Local validation on Python 3.12.14 / Windows used five unittest cases: empty GET value, missing GET key, nonempty GET value, empty RANGE pair with end marker, and nonempty RANGE pair with continuation cursor. Base: 2 fail / 3 pass. With the candidate change: all 5 pass. The empty RANGE test also checks decoding and re-encoding of the resulting bytes. git diff --check passes. Native server and full integration tests were not run.

Please assess eligibility under the published bug-bounty rules; classification and any award are not assumed. I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits, not cash.

leads.title: Senior Software Engineer -  Ruby on Rails

Most of the work comes down to one thing: making the product better. We modernise the stack as we go, moving from Rails + Ember.js to Rails + Hotwire. There's deeper technical work alongside it, on performance, stability, and the platform, all in service of a product that feels faster and more reliable. Our long-term aim is to get closer to our users by shipping faster, moving from one monthly release with regular hotfixes toward continuous delivery. What you'll do: Join one of our engineering squads and own full-stack delivery on the roadmap, from backend logic and database design to the server-rendered UI it connects to Lead the migration of Ember features to Rails + Hotwire, which means understanding the existing functionality, redesigning it thoughtfully together with PMs/designers, and shipping something better than what was there before Handle support escalations and legacy bug-fixing as part of the mix alongside feature work. The balance will depend on which squad you join, but keeping the codebase healthy and customers unblocked is part of the job Contribute to improving our CI/CD practices and deployment pipeline as we work toward more frequent, more reliable releases Keep performance in mind across the stack Build and maintain integrations with Learning Management Systems using LTI and partner APIs Participate in code reviews and technical design discussions, bringing both quality standards and a pragmatist's sense of what's worth the effort What you bring: You have 5+ years of professional software engineering experience and Ruby on Rails is your home stack: you've shipped production code with it, you know its conventions, and you're comfortable in its edges You write tests as a matter of course, not as an afterthought. RSpec and Capybara are part of your regular toolkit, and you write tests that actually catch things rather than just confirm the happy path You are user-oriented: when you're deciding how a feature should work, your first instinct is to think about the person using it, not the implementation that's most convenient You've worked in a legacy codebase before and come through it well. You know what to fix, what to leave, and how to leave things better than you found them without getting stuck in a refactoring spiral You understand CI/CD well enough to work within good practices and to nudge a codebase toward them when they're missing You communicate clearly, give honest feedback in code reviews, and take it just as well. leads.title: Deep Learning Engineer
leads.description: Your next mission Train the intelligence behind our radars – turning complex signal data into instant, real-world detection. As our Deep Learning Engineer, you develop, optimize, and deploy neural networks that enhance real-time radar performance. You work side-by-side with AI, Software Engineering, Hardware, and Product Management colleagues – translating abstract radar signal modalities into models that spot small airborne objects in noisy environments. You report to the Team Lead AI, and your models directly safeguard critical sites around the globe. What you'll do Model design and architecture: Design, train, and optimize deep learning models for detection, segmentation, and classification. Tailor neural networks to process abstract, non-natural 3D, 4D, and 5D radar imagery. Target classification and tracking: Build advanced neural network architectures to detect and track small objects like birds and drones. Ensure models perform reliably despite real-world background noise and weather. Data engineering and automation: Prepare, preprocess, and augment large-scale radar datasets for training pipelines. Implement automated labeling strategies to streamline data preparation at scale. Edge optimization and deployment: Optimize trained neural networks for high-performance inference on edge computing hardware. Collaborate with Software Developers and Radar Specialists to integrate models seamlessly into production systems. Research and field validation: Evaluate emerging deep learning techniques to continuously lift our radar capabilities. Test model robustness under diverse field conditions and document design choices clearly. What you bring MSc in Data Science, Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, or a related technical field 2-4 years of experience in Deep Learning, specifically within Computer Vision Strong proficiency in Python and hands-on experience using PyTorch Practical experience with edge deployment and model optimization tools like TensorRT or ONNX Familiarity with non-natural signal modalities such as radar, sonar, LiDAR, or medical imaging Fluent English, both written and spoken A proactive mindset and strong problem-solving skills in a collaborative environment What we offer Working for a Great Place to Work® certified company; Comprehensive pension plan; Commuting allowance; 30 days of paid holiday leave (with the possibility to buy 3 additional days); Opportunities to develop your skills even further through training and certifications; High quality laptop/desktop, monitor, headphones, and any other equipment necessary for your role; An international team of 30+ nationalities, full of high performance colleagues you can exchange experiences with and learn from. As well as having a lot of fun in our social events and Friday drinks! Robin Radar is a defence technology leader in detecting, tracking and classifying drones and other small airborne objects. Our radars and software protect military sites, borders and critical infrastructure from drone threats, and also help prevent bird strikes in aviation and reduce the impact of wind farms on wildlife. Our work shows up at defence and security sites, airports and wind farms around the world. We're one of the top 10 fastest-growing companies in the Netherlands, with a crew of bright minds across 30+ nationalities. Growth doesn't mean we lose the plot – eyes on the skies, feet on the ground. Our values keep us grounded: WE TRUST. WE OWN IT. WE AIM HIGH. Want to work on next-level radar tech, solve real problems, and never have to pretend your job has meaning? You'll fit right in – we're saving you a seat. leads.description:
# HER Hack-Astron # 7 | Spark-X2.6 Open Source AI for Good Challenge

Build something useful for people who need it. This round invites you to use **Spark-X2.6-4B** to create a working application for disaster response, health, accessibility, gender equality, or another public-interest need.

**Go to [Spark-X2.6-4B on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B), give the model a ❤️ Like, and download and use it to build your application. Publish your complete project with a video or illustrated demo in the model's Hugging Face Community Discussions, then reply to this event Issue with the Discussion link.**

- Model and getting started: https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B
- Publish your project (Hugging Face Community Discussions): https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B/discussions
- Submit your Discussion link (reply to this event Issue): https://github.com/XHToken/Spark-X2.6/issues/16

## Quick Summary

1. Individuals of any gender are welcome. For team entries, at least 50% of contributors must identify as women, following the HER Hack-Astron participation rule.
2. Your application must actually use Spark-X2.6-4B. Explain what the model does in the application.
3. Every submission must include **a video demo OR an illustrated demo with screenshots and explanatory text** showing the application running.
4. Publish the complete entry in Spark-X2.6-4B's Hugging Face Community Discussions, then reply to this announcement Issue with the direct Discussion link.
5. AI-assisted development is allowed; disclose how it was used. AI personas must not be presented as human participants.
6. No live presentation is required.
7. One winner receives **USD 100**. No upfront participation or prize-claim fee is required.

## Schedule

- Submissions open: **October 23, 2026 (UTC)**
- Submission deadline: **October 31, 2026, 23:59 UTC**
- Beijing time equivalent of the deadline: **November 1, 2026, 07:59 (UTC+8)**
- Judging and winner announcement: after submissions close; updates will be posted in this Issue.

**UTC is the authoritative time zone for the event.**

## Challenge Tracks

Choose one or combine several. Other applications with a clear public benefit are also welcome.

- **Disaster preparedness and response**: organize public emergency information, structure requests for assistance, match supply information, or support multilingual communication.
- **Health and well-being**: explain health education materials in plain language, support appointment preparation, or help users keep health and care records.
- **Accessibility**: simplify complex text, assist with reading and communication, or help people navigate public services.
- **Gender equality**: identify and explain gender bias in text, improve access to support resources, or create tools supporting equal participation in education and employment.
- **Other public-interest applications**: elder support, inclusive education, environmental protection, community mutual aid, or volunteer coordination.

Focus on a specific group of users and a concrete problem. Show how your application helps them and where its limitations remain.

## How to Participate

1. Visit [Spark-X2.6-4B on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B), click **❤️ Like**, and follow the model card to download and run the model.
2. Build a working application that uses Spark-X2.6-4B. Record the model revision, runtime, hardware, precision or quantization, and key inference settings. If using a mirror, identify the source and corresponding revision.
3. Prepare **one of the following required demo formats**:
   - **Video demo**: a screen recording showing the scenario, user input, application workflow, and actual output. A duration of 2–5 minutes is recommended.
   - **Illustrated demo**: screenshots with step-by-step explanations showing the same end-to-end workflow. Include actual inputs and outputs.
   
   Concept slides, promotional images, or descriptions without a running demonstration are insufficient.
4. Create a **new Discussion in [Spark-X2.6-4B's Hugging Face Community](https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B/discussions)**. Include `HER Hack-Astron # 7` in the title, for example: `[HER Hack-Astron # 7] [Open Source AI for Good] <Project name>`.

   Publish the complete project description, video or illustrated demo, model usage, and reproduction instructions in that Discussion. Embed screenshots or provide publicly accessible video links, and check that reviewers can access them.
5. Reply to **[this event's GitHub Issue](https://github.com/XHToken/Spark-X2.6/issues/16)** with the direct Discussion link, for example: `https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B/discussions/<number>`. This completes your submission. For team entries, also list all contributors and their profiles in your reply. Keep subsequent project updates in the same Discussion.

**Submission requires both steps: publish the complete project in the designated Hugging Face Community Discussion, then leave its link in this event's GitHub Issue. GitHub-only or other-platform-only submissions are not accepted.**

leads.title: Show HN: PatchWave - Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot
leads.description: Hey Hacker News, we're Ben, Josh, and Donnie, co-founders of PatchWave. PatchWave is a GitHub App that combines static analysis and eval'ed agents to analyze and (optionally) auto-merge PRs it deems as safe. If a Dependabot PR breaks your CI build, a fix agent works to get CI passing again. Dependabot PRs suck. Nobody likes dealing with them. Most of the time they go ignored or a senior engineer spends their valuable time dealing with them. Before PatchWave, I ran a freelance business charging clients hourly to do exactly this kind of "keep the lights on" work. Even at our small startup, we'd spend Monday mornings dealing with Dependabot PRs. Having a human-in-the-loop working with an agent on these PRs was time consuming and, often, agents would get lazy and not actually validate how an upstream change affected the codebase. And, as the quantity and severity of CVEs increases, merging security updates quickly becomes increasingly important. PatchWave is a set of specialized agents that uses static analysis tools on context we gather deterministically. 1. We pull the changelog, the code diff between versions, security advisories, and CI results. 2. The agent checks out your code in an isolated sandbox, where it uses structural code search, type checkers and your project's own toolchain to understand how your codebase uses each dependency being updated. Every Dependabot PR gets a report. You can see a few examples (against OSS repos) here: https://reports.patchwave.ai/alam00000/bentopdf/pull/913 and https://reports.patchwave.ai/shipshapecode/shepherd/pull/355... 3. If CI fails, we automatically dispatch a fix agent to try to get CI green again. For most PRs, this means updating your code to use a newer API, fixing linting/formatting issues, etc. 4. We have an optional feature that allows auto-merging certain PRs when PatchWave deems them as safe and the PR aligns with your auto-merge policy. Our recommended auto-merge policy is to auto-merge patch/minor/major dev dependencies and patch/minor production dependencies. You can customize this policy or turn auto-merge off entirely. PatchWave will skip auto-merge in a bunch of cases where a human should review. For instance, if provenance changes (e.g., a package that's usually published by GitHub Actions via Trusted Publishing is suddenly published by an API Key), we require human review before merging. Dependabot also instituted an on-by-default 3-day cooldown to reduce the risk of supply chain attacks. If PatchWave makes any changes via a fix agent, we'll always require your review before merge. Currently, PatchWave only works with Dependabot and GitHub. We plan to offer Renovate support in the future. We've eval'ed the agents the most against TypeScript and Ruby, but are always adding to our eval suite to improve accuracy. The fix agent works best with PRs that require modest code changes. For large updates, especially updates that span multiple majors, our fix agent will give up and provide you a remediation plan to help you mitigate. On the privacy/security side of the house, our SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress (see trust.contextbridge.ai). We only run on repos you select, our agents run in a short-lived microVM per run, we use Amazon Bedrock with zero-data-retention, and never train on your code. We're offering 25 free PRs per GitHub org, per month with no credit card required. Additional PRs are billed at about $1/PR, with discounts for higher volume. We also would love to accelerate OSS projects, so reach out to ask about additional free credits. If you hate dealing with Dependabot PRs, we'd love for you to give it a shot and tell us what you think. Josh, Donnie, and I will be around answering any questions and responding to any feedback you have.

leads.title: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 ( https://agent37.com ). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox. You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses. One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings. Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month. Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost: * When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost. * Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost. * Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators. * And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host. We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques. Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff. I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya. If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform. Thanks! https://agent37.com

leads.title: Wiki-driven development: coding agents update a wiki for you, you set direction
leads.description: My team has been working in a way we are calling calling wiki-driven development, where the wiki is written for the human, not the agent and the human uses primarily the wiki to set direction for the agent. This is different from Karparthy's LLm I'm curious whether others do something like it. Once I run several coding agents at a time, I get overwhelmed and disorganized. Every session makes decisions and raises questions, and I can't reread the transcripts. CLAUDE.md and agent memory help the agent, but they don't give me a place to see what is going on and decide. The problem gets worse with a team. So, I have the agents write a wiki, and they write it for me. As they work, they record only what is significant: decisions with who made them, when, and the option we passed over; open questions with an owner; and a short summary of where each area stands. I ask it to focus on the big picture, strategy, key architectural or business decisions. In more detail: 1. Agents do the work and update the pages it affects with what is significant: key decisions, key strategic points, open questions, and a summary of where things stand. 2. I read the wiki to understand the big picture: the key points, where we are, and what still needs to be decided. It is short enough to read. 3. I think and decide there: I settle a question, change a decision, lay out some more strategy points, or rewrite a page to say where I want to go. 4. The next session builds from the page I changed. Karpathy's LLM Wiki idea is related, but it compiles sources you collect into a knowledge base that keeps getting richer. His goal is completeness for research. Our approach is minimalistic: the pages distill way down from the agents' sessions, hold only what is significant, and exist only so I can think and decide. Spec-driven development has you write the spec up front for the agent to implement. Here the agent writes the wiki based on all the valuable detail that are in my session prompts and its response and I edit the wiki, so the document keeps up with the agents work and my job is thinking, organizing, deciding, direction. Here are some things I have learned doing this: - Organization is key for me as the human. I make the agent make a nice visual html with clickable links marketecture or architecture or business model canvas as the top page and navigate from there. I have it keep each page a page long so I actually am motivated to read stuff. - Have the decisions record the rejected options, so when someone brings a question back, the reasoning is available. We are constantly revisiting decisions as we work and learn and so this is very helpful. - The agent wants to write everything down. The criteria I give it is to only record what it would need to get back to where we are right now in terms of strategy, decisions, implementation. Its not that much. You can do the same with a CLAUDE.md that tells the agent what to record, and work in markdown files or Obsidian or Notion. We got so into this that we turned it into a free, MIT-licensed plugin for Claude Code and Codex that keeps the wiki as markdown files in your repo and lets you see the wiki in your browser locally: https://github.com/nimbalyst/nimbalyst-wiki. Do you work in this way? If so, what other things should we be doing and how have you made it work well?

leads.title: Show HN: I paid Claude US$1,070 to read the worst reviews of 30k places to stay
leads.description: Hi HN, I'm Oriol, a solo developer in Barcelona. Before booking anything, I used to do the same thing every time: find a place with a great rating, open the lowest-rated reviews and read them one by one. Broken AC, thin walls, a bed as hard as a board, a shower that barely works. Very often the deal-breaker was right there, written by guest after guest, under a lovely 8.9 global score. OKstays does that reading for you. It scores 33,000+ places to stay in 95 destinations on how well you'll actually sleep and stay there, and ranks them for how you travel (light sleeper, remote work, family...). This month I re-scored 30,500 places from what guests wrote. For each one, Claude reads its newest and lowest-rated reviews, then a second search collects what about 7 other review and booking sites say. It scores 67 comfort signals from 0 to 10, each with a short reason you can read on the place's page. If a deal-breaker (dirty rooms, an uncomfortable bed, a poor shower, bugs) ends up at 6.0 or below, the place is left out of every ranking. One angry guest can't do that alone: it has to be a pattern. What came out (method and charts: https://okstays.com/stats/deal-breakers ): - 1 in 39 places to stay has a deal-breaker guests keep reporting. - Half of them come down to a poor shower (51%). leads.description:
## 📝 Background

ttnn.softmax_in_place and ttnn.scale_mask_softmax_in_place can silently return incorrect results for height-sharded inputs when used with SoftmaxShardedMultiCoreProgramConfig and the shard grid does not begin at core (0, 0). On affected offset grids, some shards are softmaxed while others are left unchanged with their input logits. The same failure pattern is reproducible on Wormhole and Blackhole in ttsim.

This is a correctness issue: the operation returns without an error, but the output can be substantially wrong. Sharded layer_norm and rms_norm on comparable offset grids are correct.
## 🎯 What Success Looks Like

    Fix both softmax_in_place and scale_mask_softmax_in_place for supported height-sharded inputs whose shard grid is offset from (0, 0).

    Fix both softmax_in_place and scale_mask_softmax_in_place for supported height-sharded inputs whose shard grid is offset from (0, 0).
    Add regression coverage for height-sharded inputs on grids at (0, 0), (1, 0), and (0, 1), covering both ROW_MAJOR and COL_MAJOR orientations, with and without a mask.

    Add regression coverage for height-sharded inputs on grids at (0, 0), (1, 0), and (0, 1), covering both ROW_MAJOR and COL_MAJOR orientations, with and without a mask.
    Compare the output shard by shard against the corresponding PyTorch softmax result (including the masked result for scale_mask_softmax_in_place) using the repository's established correctness tolerances. Verify that every shard is updated and correct, not merely that the operation returns successfully.

    Compare the output shard by shard against the corresponding PyTorch softmax result (including the masked result for scale_mask_softmax_in_place) using the repository's established correctness tolerances. Verify that every shard is updated and correct, not merely that the operation returns successfully.
    Preserve correct behavior for origin-based shard grids and the existing supported configurations.

    Preserve correct behavior for origin-based shard grids and the existing supported configurations.
    The focused regression tests pass on the applicable TT hardware/simulator test target, and the PR passes required CI. Document any unrelated known simulator failures separately rather than expanding this bounty to cover them.

    The focused regression tests pass on the applicable TT hardware/simulator test target, and the PR passes required CI. Document any unrelated known simulator failures separately rather than expanding this bounty to cover them.
    The change is reviewed and approved by the relevant engineering team before merge.

    The change is reviewed and approved by the relevant engineering team before merge.

## 💡 Problem to Solve

The shared validate_sharded_input validation accepts an offset shard grid after comparing its bounding-box dimensions against compute_with_storage_grid_size. The sharded softmax factory, however, currently constructs its work range from (0, 0) and enumerates per-core runtime arguments from the origin. This can launch work on cores outside the input shard grid while leaving actual shards on offset cores untouched.

Update the host-side sharded softmax program setup so its work units and per-core runtime arguments correspond to the input tensor's shard grid and its orientation. leads.title: [Bounty $750] Fix remaining sharded scale_mask_softmax mask handling issues
leads.description:
📝 Background

ttnn.scale_mask_softmax_in_place with SoftmaxShardedMultiCoreProgramConfig can hang or read incorrect mask values when the input shard layout and mask shape/specification do not align. These cases can break correctness in sharded attention workloads and may hang the device instead of returning a clear validation error.

An open change already addresses the causal-mask case where a shard is shorter than or not divisible by the mask height, and the causal mask/input batch-size mismatch. This bounty is for the remaining issues below; coordinate with that change and do not duplicate its scope: [PR #63692](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/pull/63692).

🎯 What Success Looks Like

A row-major mask combined with is_causal_mask=True is either handled correctly or rejected during validation with a clear error before device execution; it must not hang.

Causal interleaved mask readers wrap rows using the mask’s height, not the input width. Non-square causal masks produce correct results without out-of-bounds reads.

Mask addressing remains correct when a shard crosses a batch boundary; the batch cursor must not advance early or read beyond the mask tensor.

A sharded mask with an incompatible shard specification (including shard orientation) is rejected clearly or handled correctly; it must not silently read a different core’s shard.

Add regression tests for each addressed case, covering valid configurations and invalid configurations as appropriate. Compare supported outputs against a PyTorch reference.

Existing relevant sharded and causal softmax tests continue to pass, and existing supported configurations retain their behavior.

💡 Problem to Solve

The sharded softmax factory, mask readers, and validation do not consistently enforce or honor the assumptions used to walk masks:

A row-major mask with is_causal_mask=True can select a reader that does not follow the causal compute’s per-row mask consumption, causing a hang.

Causal interleaved readers can wrap mask rows using the input width rather than the mask height, leading to incorrect/out-of-bounds reads for non-square masks.

When a shard spans a batch boundary, integer division in the per-batch core calculation can make mask addressing advance to the next batch too early.

Validation checks mask layout and padded shape but does not ensure that a sharded mask’s shard specification matches the input’s expected distribution.

leads.title: Spent 5 months on an enterprise deal, only to lose the deal to the CPO's buddy
leads.description: I have a startup in the AI Agents domain, which is an extremely competitive space with 100s of similar products. However, we differentiate by focusing a bit more on enterprises, data compliance, PII encryption, and serverless / self-hosted setups. Because of this, we generally work closely with a client's tech team rather than their customer support team. In May, we received an inbound inquiry from a multi-billion dollar company. Our first meeting went great. They loved our product, and we went ahead with multiple demos, signed NDAs etc. Eventually, they evaluated our compliance. Our ISO 27001 certification was still in progress at the time, so they asked us to wait until it was finished. We worked very hard throughout the month of June and successfully got our certificate, complying with almost 220 items. We reconnected in mid-July and they started testing. I gave them a lot of options, and we were continuously working on different versions of the product together. We kept this momentum going from July until mid-August. Suddenly, from mid-August onward, their team's interest seemed to drop off randomly. They stopped responding to our emails and went completely quiet. Later on, I reached out to a friend who works internally at that organization to see what happened. I found out that their CPO had recommended a different company, so the team migrated to them. Just like that, 5 to 6 months of my effort were wasted. They haven't even officially informed me yet. My contact told me that because their volume of work is so high, they might have a demand for us in the future and want to keep us around as an option - but for now, they have gone with the CPO's seller. What did I do wrong while closing this enterprise SaaS client?

leads.title: feat(health): sport ensemble — routes HealthKit, localisation téléphone et bonus de groupe
leads.description:
**Pourquoi** — Permettre au joueur de faire reconnaître une vraie séance commune, même avec une montre sans route, puis montrer le bonus signature de **GRRIND**. Cadrage métier/serveur : [grrind-back#329](https://github.com/younesdiouri/grrind-back/issues/329), source de vérité.

## Règles à afficher

1 / 2 / 3 / 4+ joueurs distincts, soi compris → **×1 / ×2 / ×3 / ×4**. Même sport normalisé, ≥80 % de chevauchement pour chaque séance, proximité d'environ 100 m. **L'auteur a choisi un multiplicateur après le plafond quotidien** : 100 XP solo après plafond → 300 XP à trois. Le serveur tranche tout ; le client ne calcule ni proximité, ni groupe, ni XP.

## Périmètre, dans cet ordre

- [ ] **Spike terrain d'abord** : étendre le module Swift `modules/grrind-health` pour lire les `HKWorkoutRoute` autorisées, par lots, avec horodatage et précision. Une route peut arriver après le workout : prévoir la relance d'enrichissement sans rejouer le crédit. Identifier concrètement les montres/apps qui remontent une route exploitable.
- [ ] **Solution sans route** : proposer « Sport ensemble » avant la séance pour activer la collecte de localisation du téléphone. Explication courte de l'utilité, permissions demandées au bon moment, état actif visible, arrêt explicite et arrêt de sécurité borné. Collecter pendant la séance, y compris écran verrouillé/arrière-plan selon les capacités réelles d'iOS ; documenter interruption/arrêt forcé. Une position prise après le sport ne prouve rien.
- [ ] La capture de positions ne crée aucun workout ni chronomètre de jeu. Le workout vient toujours de la santé. Rapprocher la capture du workout de **son compte** via les données fournisseur et ses bornes ; aucun sport normalisé, durée ou multiplicateur déclaré par l'app.
- [ ] Persister les lots en attente et leurs identifiants, reprendre après réseau coupé/app relancée, envoyer les preuves indépendamment de l'import lorsque le contrat existe. Préserver `Idempotency-Key` et la réponse originale du lot santé ; pas de GPS dans les logs. Purger dès remise utile et au plus 30 jours après la séance.
- [ ] Refus/révocation de localisation, GPS approximatif ou route absente : l'import et l'XP solo fonctionnent. Montrer le statut serveur « preuve insuffisante » ou « en attente », sans affirmer que le joueur était seul ni promettre un bonus acquis.
- [ ] **Contrat back d'abord** : tirer `openapi.yaml` depuis main puis générer les types. Le back fournira statut, nombre de joueurs, multiplicateur et XP avant/après/supplément. Aucun endpoint, DTO ni enum serveur inventé ici ; préparer la partie native indépendante pendant l'attente.
- [ ] Bilan et historique : afficher « Sport ensemble ×N » et le supplément **serveur**. Conserver le bilan agrégé actuel du lot ; ne pas appliquer un multiplicateur global à des séances de groupes différents. Les compléments accordés après la synchro d'un ami se présentent une seule fois, via leurs identifiants stables et paliers serveur, sans rejouer l'ancien `SyncSummary`.
- [ ] Texte permission/explication : « GRRIND utilise ta localisation pendant cette séance pour reconnaître le sport ensemble. » Ajouter les libellés et traductions selon les conventions existantes ; aucun ancien nom d'app.

## Validation

- [ ] Sur les appareils réels utilisés : montre avec/sans route, intérieur/extérieur, téléphone verrouillé/arrière-plan, GPS refusé/imprécis, offline/reprise et ami qui synchronise plus tard. Témoins négatifs : simple croisement, horaires/sports différents, personnes éloignées.

leads.title: Show HN: Vu – a new programming language designed for AI. Rust speeds, Py syntax
leads.description: hi everyone! I wanted to share what I've been working on these past 6~ years. TL;DR: Rust is great, but somewhere along the way, I learned that I was too dumb to read and write Rust. As I worked on larger and larger Rust projects, I also became frustrated with the developer experience of working in Rust (slow compile time), so I wanted a better way. Vu's language changed a bit over time but the core principles remained the same: 1. It should be easy to read and write 2. It should be memory safe 3. It should be fast to run 4. It should be fast to compile Here's how I approached each: 1. Vu is syntactically very close to Python. The ownership rules are the ones Rust has, but I personally find it a lot easier to parse and understand. I've tested this with various LLMs and found it can read and write Vu out the box because of the similarity to Python. 2. Vu uses the same principles of Rust. Every value has one owner, borrows can't escape or outlive what they borrow, and nothing changes while it's borrowed. 3. Vu compiles down to C at the end of the day, so everything runs approximately at C speeds. 4. vuc check on the compiler’s own source (about 21,500 lines of Vu), takes about 0.4~ s. This check covers parsing, type and borrow checking. cargo check on a Rust project that size usually takes several seconds from scratch. Then there are other opinionated language decisions. Vu has no macros, Vu's borrow checker is lighter weight than Rust's with simpler interfaces and generics. However, in the past few years, as Vu's language evolved and AI began to take over, I expanded Vu's principles to include a couple additional principles: 5. It should be secure 6. It should be efficient for LLMs to write 5. I want to pen test Vu in public. In https://github.com/vu0tran/vu/tree/main/tests , you'll see a battery of tests where I'm trying to basically pwn Vu. There are explicit language decisions in there as well that tries to prevent a host of security flaws that exist in other languages, e.g, integer overflow stops the program instead of quietly wrapping around. 6. The syntax of Vu is designed to be tokenizer efficient. In addition, when Vu checks throws errors, the errors are designed to be token efficient and written in a way that guides LLMs to more easily fix bugs, reducing turns overall. So, in summary, Vu is still experimental. The compiler is 21,500 lines of Vu and compiles itself. The standard library also has TLS, HTTP/2, WebSockets and a PostgreSQL client, all tested against Python’s implementations and hostile input. I think most of the pieces are there. It does also compile down also to WebAssembly so you can play around w/ the checker on the website! Feel free to try to break it! What's next: 1. Figure out how to get Vu to perform faster than Rust 2. Rewrite some OSS libraries in Vu to further prove the language

Comment "taking this" and wait to be assigned; only the assigned person is paid. If there is no pull request within 7 days, the maintainer unassigns it and the task opens up again. leads.description: It's not on their website or Trust center yet, but we received the following breach notification from WorkOS: We are writing to notify you of a data security incident that we detected on October 30, 2026 and are continuing to investigate. We value your trust and want to keep you informed while our investigation continues. What Happened On October 30, 2026, at 16:39 UTC, WorkOS detected anomalous traffic to an internal business system. Our investigation identified evidence the attack was likely driven by ARTEX, an AI-assisted, autonomous penetration testing framework, from IP addresses based in Hong Kong and China. The unauthorized actor gained access to an internal API used by our sales and marketing tools. Through this service, it was able to access data from our Salesforce and Snowflake instances. These systems hold business contact information, account and commercial information, aggregated and de-identified product usage metrics, marketing contacts, and support tickets. This includes CRM information such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, company mailing addresses, and other business information for WorkOS customers. We have no evidence that your application data was accessed. We also have no evidence that any production WorkOS services were accessed or impacted. Our current analysis indicates this incident was localized to only CRM and customer support data. ...

leads.title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
leads.description: If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn not to enter confidential information . https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988 “[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“ https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review “A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers” https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data “Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. Instead, they are retained for up to three years.” https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_data_usage “Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.” To disable their training on your chat sessions, you need to turn off “Keep Activity” in Gemini’s settings. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours. I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough. Thank you to this user on HN for mentioning in another thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50355424
