leads.title: Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) C-UAS
leads.description: EMPLOYER IS A CONTRACTOR FOR THE U.S. GOVERNMENT. THIS POSITION REQUIRES U.S. CITIZENSHIP. Role Description This is a forward-deployed engineering role . You'll work shoulder-to-shoulder with mission heroes- the users, operators, and program engineers who run real workloads in real DoD environments- and lead the software integration of modular Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems (C-UAS) sensors and effectors. You will deploy, harden, integrate, and operate our modular C-UAS solution. Forward-deployed means aligned with the mission hero , not always on a plane . Most of the work is remote. You'll travel to sites when the engagement genuinely calls for it — initial standup, in-SCIF integration work, on-the-ground incident response, training, and knowledge transfer- and you'll be on a video call or in a shared chat with that same mission hero the rest of the time. The job is being their engineer, not living at their desk. You are a cross-functional engineering leader. You can take responsibility for the full breadth of a data and software integration platform- make it work where it has to work, analyze what's running through it, and solve problems in real time for the mission hero. About 20% of your time, you'll also help make Defense Unicorns ' forward-deployed team better — pairing with junior Data Engineer FDEs on hard problems, helping them develop technical judgment, and raising the ceiling on what the team can take on. Responsibilities Deploy and harden UDS Data Capability in the mission hero's environment — stand up UDS Store (Iceberg, Rook/Ceph, pgvector, Postgres), wire up UDS Transit for air-gap data movement, configure UDS Govern policies (Pepr/Lula), and integrate UDS Connect (Strimzi/Kafka) where streaming or legacy connectors are required. Own integration with existing mission systems — connect UDS Data Capability to existing infrastructure, including sensor arrays, computer-vision-enabled UAS interceptors, and a broad range of C-UAS solutions. Build pipelines that move data through classification boundaries — ingestion, transformation, catalog registration, model/dataset packaging via Zarf, cross-domain transit, and eventual consistency across DDIL conditions. Operate what you deploy — own initial day-2 operations, including capacity, performance, backup/restore (Velero), observability (Vector/Loki), incident response, and upgrade paths. Transition ownership to the mission hero's operations team once stable. Generate accreditation artifacts — STIG evidence, cATO documentation, FIPS validation notes, and policy mappings to support ISSM/ISSO requirements in IL4/IL5 environments. Represent the mission hero to product and engineering — document issues, write postmortems, recommend operator improvements, and communicate field challenges to the platform engineering team. Train and transfer knowledge — develop runbooks, architecture documentation, working sessions, and knowledge-transfer materials that enable mission teams to operate independently. Mentor junior Data Engineer FDEs — pair on complex problems, review integration designs, and help engineers develop technical judgment without direct people-management responsibilities. Clearance & Travel Clearance: Active TS/SCI required. Travel: Approximately 10%–25%, based on mission and customer requirements. On-site expectations: Ability to work in SCIFs and other restricted environments for days or weeks when required for integration, incident response, training, or knowledge transfer. Most work is performed remotely. Required Qualifications Experience working in tactical edge and interoperable mission environments, including TAK Server administration, ATAK/WinTAK, tactical communications, and disconnected or air-gapped systems. Production experience with modern data platforms, including lakehouse technologies (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, or Hudi), object storage (Ceph or S3-compatible), PostgreSQL, and analytical query engines such as Trino, DuckDB, ClickHouse, or Spark SQL.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python wire client rejects valid responses larger than 16 KiB (e.g., LBS GET with block size > 16360)
leads.description:
## Python wire client rejects valid responses larger than 16 KiB (e.g., LBS GET with block size > 16360)

At `3de151b` (`master`), `tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py` defines

    MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES = 16384

with the comment "This is a somewhat arbitrary value", and `Wire.send_recv()` reads the whole response with a single bounded call:

    idnum, record = split_packet(self.sock.recv(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES))

`split_packet()` then requires the *entire* frame inside that one buffer:

    record, crc = struct.unpack_from('>%dsI' % record_length, packet, offset=16)
    assert len(packet) == len(record) + 16 + 4

A Wire frame for a record of length `N` is `N + 20` bytes, so any response record longer than 16364 bytes cannot be processed: `recv()` returns at most 16384 bytes and `struct.unpack_from` raises `struct.error`.

This is separate from #358 (responses fragmented across reads of a small packet). PR #359's stated fix explicitly keeps "the existing total response-size limit", so this bug remains even after #359 is merged.

### Valid server responses that exceed the cap

1. **LBS GET with block size > 16360.** The block size is operator-configured via `lbs -b`, validated to `[PROTO_LBS_BLKLEN_MIN, PROTO_LBS_BLKLEN_MAX]` = `[512, 131072]` (`lbs/main.c`, `lib/proto_lbs/proto_lbs.h`). An LBS GET response record is `4 (status) + blklen` bytes (`lib/proto_lbs/proto_lbs_server.c`, `proto_lbs_response_get()`). Any deployment configured with block size ≥ 16361 — legal up to the documented maximum of 131072 — produces GET responses the Python client cannot read. The C server imposes no such limit: `proto_lbs_request_parse()` `malloc()`s APPEND payloads dynamically and `wire_writepacket_getbuf()` sizes GET responses to the configured block size.

2. **KVLDS RANGE responses.** The response record grows with the data returned: `4 (status) + 4 (num_pairs) + nextkey + Σ(1+keylen + 1+valen)` (each pair up to 514 bytes). For 100-byte keys/values, a range response with roughly 80 pairs already exceeds the cap; `tests/python/dump_kvlds.py` requests `maxsize = 8192` pairs per range call, so the dump tool fails on most non-trivial datasets. The C-side range response is likewise dynamically sized.

### Reproduction (real C server, no mocks)

On `3de151b`, with `crcmod` installed:

    $ ./lbs/lbs -s /tmp/repro/lbs.sock -d /tmp/repro/storage -b 32768 -1 &
    $ python3 - <<'EOF'
    import sys
    sys.path.insert(0, 'tests/python')
    from kivaloo import proto_lbs
    p = proto_lbs.Proto_lbs('/tmp/repro/lbs.sock')
    print("params():", p.params())
    data = bytes(range(256)) * 128          # one 32 KiB block
    print("append():", p.append(1, 0, data))
    print("get():", p.get(0))
    EOF

    params(): (32768, 0)
    append(): 0 1
    get() FAILED -> error: unpack_from requires a buffer of at least 32792 bytes
        for unpacking 32776 bytes at offset 16 (actual buffer size is 16384)

The C `lbs` server accepts the 32 KiB block and serves it (no server-side error); only the Python client fails.

### Impact

- The Python client cannot interoperate with any LBS deployment configured with block size > 16360 (legal up to 131072).
- `dump_kvlds.py` and any KVLDS RANGE consumer fail once a range response exceeds 16 KiB.
- The test suite cannot exercise the C server with non-default (larger) block sizes, because the harness itself rejects the responses.

### Suggested fix

In `send_recv()`: read the 16-byte header first (as #359 proposes), then read exactly `record_length + 4` further bytes based on the header's `record_length` field before calling `split_packet()`. This bounds the allocation by the protocol maximum (LBS: 20 + 4 + 131072 = 131096 bytes; KVLDS: bounded by the requested data) instead of a fixed 16384. `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` can then be removed or raised to the protocol maximum.

### Scope / disclosure

This report is limited to the Python client/helper and its callers (`tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py`). I am not reporting a crash in the C storage server, a security exploit, or stored-data corruption. The C client (`lib/wire/wire_readpacket.c`) reads complete packets and is unaffected.

This report, investigation and reproduction were prepared by an LLM with the authorization of the `zhangb06` account owner. I am available to discuss the problem or a fix through this account. No live customer data, external service testing, or payment credentials were used.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python LBS append silently truncates or pads mismatched block counts
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), submitting on behalf of the account owner. I can help discuss this reproduction and revise the candidate patch in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/proto_lbs.py:Proto_lbs.append() checks that the byte length is a multiple of the block size, but not that it matches nums * block_size. The actual Wire.send_recv() then uses a fixed-length struct.pack string field, silently truncating or padding mismatched data.

With block_size = 4, a recording socket under the actual Python wire encoder captured:

    nums=1 input=b'AAAABBBB' payload=b'AAAA' result=(0, 1)
    nums=2 input=b'AAAA' payload=b'AAAA\x00\x00\x00\x00' result=(0, 2)

The success responses are supplied by the socket double; no C server was run. The observed bug is the changed outgoing payload, not independently demonstrated server-side storage corruption. This requires inconsistent arguments from a caller of the Python test helper. I am not claiming an issue in the C APPEND implementation or a security vulnerability.

A candidate check, immediately after num_bytes = self.block_size * nums:

    if len(blocks) != num_bytes:
        raise ValueError("wire append: Block count does not match data length")

The following test uses the actual Proto_lbs.append, Wire.send_recv, packet encoder and decoder, with an in-memory socket double. Save as tests/python/test_lbs_append_length.py; from tests/python run python -m unittest -v test_lbs_append_length with crcmod and psutil installed.

Python 3.12.14 / Windows: baseline 1 passes and 2 fail; with the check all 3 pass. The exact-length control verifies byte preservation and the decoded success result. The mismatched cases verify no packet is sent after the fix. Full native server tests were not run.

<details><summary>Reproduction / regression test</summary>

~~~python
"""Check APPEND length validation without starting a server."""

import struct
import unittest

from kivaloo.proto_lbs import Proto_lbs
from kivaloo.wire import Wire, make_packet, split_packet


class RecordingSocket:
    def __init__(self):
        self.records = []
        self.msgnum = None

    def sendall(self, packet):
        self.msgnum, record = split_packet(packet)
        self.records.append(record)

    def recv(self, size):
        _, nums, start = struct.unpack_from('>IIQ', self.records[-1])
        return make_packet(self.msgnum, struct.pack('>IQ', 0, start + nums))

    def close(self):
        pass


class AppendLengthTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.sock = RecordingSocket()
        self.proto = Proto_lbs.__new__(Proto_lbs)
        self.proto.block_size = 4
        self.proto.wire = Wire.__new__(Wire)
        self.proto.wire.msgnum = 0
        self.proto.wire.sock = self.sock

    def tearDown(self):
        self.proto.close()

    def test_rejects_too_many_bytes(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.proto.append(1, 0, b'AAAABBBB')
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records, [])

    def test_rejects_too_few_bytes(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.proto.append(2, 0, b'AAAA')
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records, [])

    def test_exact_length_preserves_bytes(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.proto.append(2, 7, b'AAAABBBB'), (0, 9))
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records,
                         [struct.pack('>IIQ', 2, 2, 7) + b'AAAABBBB'])


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
~~~

</details>

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python wire client fails on valid responses split across stream reads
leads.description:
## Python client fails on a valid response split across stream reads

At `3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce` (`master`), `tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py:159` passes one `socket.recv(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES)` result directly to `split_packet()`. The AF_UNIX stream can return fewer bytes than a complete packet. A valid response can therefore raise an uncaught `struct.error` in the Python client even though the remaining bytes are still arriving.

This report is limited to the Python client/helper and its callers. I am **not** reporting a crash in the C storage server, a security exploit, or stored-data corruption.

### Reproduction

With the existing `crcmod` dependency installed, run this from the repository root:

```python
import sys
import struct
sys.path.insert(0, 'tests/python')
from kivaloo import wire

# A valid KVLDS PARAMS response: 8-byte payload, 28-byte complete frame.
record = struct.pack('>II', 255, 255)
packet = wire.make_packet(0, record)
assert wire.split_packet(packet) == (0, record)

class ShortReads:
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = packet
    def sendall(self, data):
        assert wire.split_packet(data) == (0, struct.pack('>I', 0x100))
    def recv(self, size):
        size = min(size, 8)
        result, self.data = self.data[:size], self.data[size:]
        return result
    def close(self):
        pass

client = wire.Wire.__new__(wire.Wire)
client.msgnum = 0
client.sock = ShortReads()
print(client.send_recv('>I', 0x100).get('>II'))
```

Expected: `(255, 255)`.

Actual on the base commit:

```text
struct.error: unpack_from requires a buffer of at least 16 bytes for
unpacking 16 bytes at offset 0 (actual buffer size is 8)
```

I also reproduced the failure using a real local `socket.socketpair()`, with an event coordinating the second fragment only after the first `recv()` returns. This needs no timing sleeps or remote service. An additional check used the compiled C `lbs` server, private temporary storage and a Unix socket: the unchanged response stream succeeds with the original client on the normal path, fails with the original client when reads are limited to eight bytes, and passes PARAMS/APPEND/GET with byte-exact data after the fix.

### Proposed fix and validation

Read the 16-byte header completely, validate its checksum and the existing total response-size limit, then read the payload and four-byte trailer completely before calling the existing `split_packet()`. Treat EOF before a full frame as an error rather than looping. Keep the existing record-checksum and response-ID checks.

A local minimal patch adds 20 lines and removes two in `wire.py`. Thirteen regression tests pass after the patch, including all 27 split points of the PARAMS response, single-byte reads, complete-response controls, early EOF, size limits, checksum failures, consecutive frames and the real socket-pair reproduction. These tests fail on the unmodified base at the framing cases. Validation used macOS arm64, Python 3.14.7 and the actual `crcmod==1.7` package. The C programs compiled successfully with the documented Homebrew OpenSSL flags; AWS/remote-service tests were not run.

Please consider this report under the published bug-bounty program if eligible. I understand that classification and any award are your decision, and that awards below $100 are account credits rather than cash. No award is assumed.

**AI disclosure and follow-up:** This report, investigation and proposed patch were prepared by OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex (LLMs), with the authorization of the `avs-io` account owner. This is not intended as a one-off report: questions and requested revisions can be addressed through this GitHub account. No live customer data, external service testing or payment credentials were used.

leads.title: Revenue Accounting Manager
leads.description: Canonical is a leading provider of open source software and operating systems to the global enterprise and technology markets. Our platform, Ubuntu, is very widely used in breakthrough enterprise initiatives such as public cloud, data science, AI, engineering innovation, and IoT. Our customers include the world's leading public cloud and silicon providers, and industry leaders in many sectors. The company is a pioneer of global distributed collaboration, with 1200+ colleagues in 75+ countries and very few office-based roles. Teams meet two to four times yearly in person, in interesting locations around the world, to align on strategy and execution. The company is founder-led, profitable, and growing. We are hiring a Revenue Accounting Manager, ideally a candidate with a passion for systems accounting, to drive revenue recognition process, decisions, systems and reporting. In our finance function we aspire to set the industry pace for speed and accuracy of reporting. We aim to achieve this by driving our product pricing and terms, contracting, sales processes and systems into alignment. We are looking for a professionally qualified accounting leader with expertise in IFRS 15/ASC 606 to build scalable contract review and revenue recognition processes. This lead will work across teams including product management, legal, FP&A, sales operations and commercial business systems to align understanding and ensure that the accounting and revenue recognition treatment of contracts and products is straightforward and correct, with a very high level of automation. Perhaps unusually we prefer a leader with deep personal interest in the software and technology industry, and ideally some data analytics and software engineering experience . The Revenue Accounting Manager will ensure the proper application of revenue accounting guidance for public market scrutiny. This is a management position which requires confidence in presentation, setting goals, and directing the work of others. We expect to grow a team focused on revenue, with a particular emphasis on systems and automation, that puts us at the top of the leaderboard for clarity, correctness, transparency and speed of reporting as a global tech company. Location: This role is home-based in EMEA time zones, with the option to be based in our London office. It will report to our Global Financial Controller. Key responsibilities Collaborate with Product Management, Sales Operations, Sales, Legal, and FP&A teams to design standard contracts Drive process and configuration improvements in NetSuite and related systems for end-to-end automation of the revenue life cycle Incorporate industry best practices and emerging technology to raise the bar for reporting speed and accuracy Review and evaluate the revenue recognition impact of non-standard contracts and new products Lead, mentor and develop a team of revenue accounting and systems accounting professionals Assist in month-end revenue close, including reconciliations, fluctuation analysis, and other reporting Develop and maintain effective internal controls over revenue transactions and reporting Research and write accounting memos on significant revenue recognition and other related policy matters Act as the primary liaison with external auditors in matters related to order-to-cash Valued skills and experience An exceptional academic track record from both high school and university An undergraduate degree in Accounting or Finance, or a compelling narrative about your alternative chosen path CPA, CA or equivalent with excellent technical accounting skills and IFRS experience A detailed understanding of IFRS 15 and relevant rules related to SaaS and services Leadership or management responsibility A track record of going above-and-beyond expectations Experience of software licensing, subscription and services revenue accounting and operations Experience driving revenue recognition and scaling accounting processes in a high-growth environment

leads.title: Recruiters told me AI screening overlooks the best candidates. True?
leads.description: After submitting a lot of CVs recently, I’ve separately been asking recruiters and hiring managers, in-house and agency, how they’re coping now that applications can be written, enhanced or fabricated by AI, and graded by AI. An in-house recruiter at a 2,000-person company said their ranking tool grades CVs A to D, and the people they end up hiring are frequently the C’s. An agency director trialled fully automated screeners and said they “overlooked some of the strongest candidates”. A hiring manager, after a run of fabricated applications, built their own grader and auto-rejects anyone who matches the job spec too closely, on the basis that no real candidate meets 100% of the requirements. I’ve seen a few similar posts along the lines of “I’d probably be rejected applying for my own job”. Everyone said most CVs now have AI involvement, many are the job spec fed back as experience, and the truth only comes out on the screening call. If you hire engineers or any other role: has the CV stopped carrying signal for you, and what are you using instead? If AI screening is actually working for you, which tool and how? I’d like the counter-examples as much as the confirmations.

leads.title: Programmer owns the architecture, AI implements crate-level modules in Rust — how does this compare to other languages?
leads.description: After working on several Rust projects with AI assistance, I want to share a division of responsibility that has worked well in practice, and ask whether others have found the same — or a better approach in other languages. The core model: The programmer owns the world-view of the project — module boundaries, crate structure, system architecture, and design trade-offs. The AI implements the flesh — concrete trait implementations, error handling, boilerplate, and module-level logic. The programmer owns the architecture; the AI owns the implementation. And the Rust compiler makes sure the two stay honest with each other. In practice, I have found that AI can already generate crate-level Rust code that compiles, runs correctly, and is architecturally sound — requiring only minor adjustments. Occasionally it produces solutions I would not have thought of myself. Why Rust works particularly well for this model: The borrow checker and type system act as a verification layer between the programmer's intent and the AI's output. If the AI misunderstands the architecture, the compiler rejects it. This means the programmer does not need to read every line of generated code — the compiler enforces the contract. This is not just about safety. It also forces the AI to produce code that is structurally honest. There is no way to paper over a bad design with runtime workarounds. Comparison with other languages: Python — The iteration cycle is fastest, and AI generates idiomatic Python reliably. But there is no compiler to catch architectural mismatches. The programmer must read and verify far more of the generated code manually. The division of responsibility is blurry. TypeScript — Static types help, and strict mode catches a meaningful class of AI mistakes. A reasonable middle ground, though AI frequently reaches for any to silence errors, weakening the contract. Go — Simple syntax reduces the surface area for AI mistakes. But nil pointer panics and verbose error handling mean AI output still requires careful review. The compiler helps less than Rust. Java — Mature static analysis tooling provides a review pipeline, but AI tends to generate verbose, over-engineered boilerplate. The null problem remains. Architecturally, the programmer ends up doing more correction work. C++ — AI can generate C++ that compiles but contains subtle memory bugs the compiler does not catch. The division of responsibility breaks down — the programmer must verify deeply, which defeats the purpose. Personal note: I came to Rust from a Java background, after also working with Go, JavaScript, Python, and C++. It took three attempts and roughly six months of serious effort before Rust clicked. What surprised me was that Rust is, in a deeper sense, a remarkably clean language. The complexity is front-loaded — concentrated at compile time — so the resulting code is predictable and self-consistent in a way that Java or C++ rarely achieves at scale. In the AGI era, that front-loaded strictness turns out to be exactly what you want when working with AI. The compiler becomes a shared contract between the programmer's world-view and the AI's implementation. Neither side can cheat. Question: Is this division of responsibility — programmer as architect, AI as implementer — viable in your experience? And does the language choice fundamentally change how well this model works? If you could only choose one language for AI-assisted development going forward, which would it be — and why?

leads.title: Show HN: Firenook – Firebase emulators in Rust: 40× faster writes, 10× less RAM
leads.description: Hi HN, we have been developing with Firebase for a long time, and the only way Firebase developers can build apps without directly costing them is using the official Firebase Emulator Suite. However, the issue with this suite is, it's dependent and running on Java with a old Console UI (not updated in years), that was not built to support tons and millions of data and has pretty bad developer experience. For a long time, we were hitting Out of Memory on even high specs laptop while developing and the worst part is while this happens all the persists data keep getting lost. We were honestly frustrated with this, and thought what if we built the Firebase Emulator Suite the right way, as it always should have been. Introducing Firenook, a faster drop-in replacement for Firebase Emulator Suite for Firebase developers. It's 40x faster writes and needs 10x less RAM to run it. We took the right approach of first building it Rust as a single engine, so that there will be no Java dependencies and built from scratch a new Console UI using modern web stacks. The result is, now we were able to run 2 millions datas loaded to Firenook with only taking around 2GB ram compared to 22GB of the official suite. Things are way faster and rebuilt Console UI gives best developer experience from logging Firebase Functions, to editing Firestore documents in JSON and many more. We developed this throughly for around 2 months now and ran this internally for a month before we decided it's time to release it to public so that other devs can make use of Firenook and also contribute it to make it better. Firenook is still new and I'm sure it misses things. So please try it our on your project and let us if there are any issues. Thank you.

leads.title: Looking for a tech job is a helpless data-entry nightmare
leads.description: I spent hundred of hours (distributed over many days) filling my resume data to freshly developed forms made specifically to the hiring process of one or two companies, even though I feel like I have a top 10% resume and years of in hands-down software development experience. I love solving problems, it's part of me. I know it has got a lot harder to land a development gig but I've worked with modern stuff like AI-generated briefs for meetings, bug logs automatically sent emails to responsible developers, at a point I had an Agent dedicated to verifying how well our code was written so I feel like I've kept up with the innovations, and skills. But I have no idea how to land a job in software development anymore: nothing seems enough. I have tried for over a year and the only reason I can withstand this much waiting while seeking a job in that field is because of my exceptional employment history (including working to Silicon Valley companies), but it has got to a point I am worried. I've asked my friends who are also developers and they feel similarly, we do not know where to dedicate our effors, as if the competency of software engineers were transformed irrelevant because of AI. We know what happened, we just don't know what to do with all the competency we embody. I've taken a liking to working as a bartender in my local city, because that's kind of the only job I can land lately, but as soon as my degree in Computer Engineering is mentioned I'm set aside as a anti-social computer expert who will never take a low-paying job like "this". (Secretly I found it very fun, fullfilling in a way I never thought I needed because money was my priority at the beggining of the carreer) How the hell do we transform this competency and learning ability of software engineers into desireable company-adding value skills? (I swear this is not generated by AI, I don't even know how to prove anymore)

leads.title: Ask HN: Techniques for productive AI use in the workspace
leads.description: Hey HN, Like so many other SWEs right now, I am trying to find ways to enhance my development experience without taking away from the quality of my work or the things I find enjoyable about software engineering, especially as one who very much enjoys the act of pulling something together using well crafted code. I have found (what I think at least) is a maximum of productivity and enjoyment by primarily using Opencode as a pair programmer and wrangling out the general structure of the solution, before doing probably a 35% AI and 65% me pass of actually writing up the code. Has anyone else found success with this technique of development? I have always been someone who very much enjoys writing well written and designed code, and I am evaluating whether I want to stay in the field as I am concerned that there will not be a place for my style of development in the future. I would appreciate it if others could share their techniques for using AI in the workplace to help me evaluate if my current methods are sustainable career-wise, if there are other ways of using AI that I may also enjoy, or if it might be time for me to look into other fields for the remainder of my career. I don't post here often so I apologize if I have violated some HN posting conventions with my post, just looking for the opinions of other developers in a place with a bit more of a pro-AI slant than the places I usually hang around.

leads.title: Show HN: Pointless but mostly-exact clone of Hacker News
leads.description: Source code: http://github.com/shawwn/sharc I had more things I wanted to do with this, but I should probably admit to myself I probably won't be. The original idea was for https://news.ycombinator.lol to be "Hacker News, but all the comments are AI." Right now it's "Hacker News, but all the comments are the same as the real HN." Hence, it's completely pointless. Special thanks to dang for collaborating -- he even suggested the name for the codebase, "sharc". Development time was about four months of near daily work: https://github.com/shawwn/sharc/tree/main/docs/agents/handof... Some days I'd spend a solid 16 hours on this. What's the point? None, really. Just to test the limits of my abilities and prove to myself that I could do what pg did. It's an extremely efficient port of HN to Common Lisp. One of the project's goals was to be high performance. According to benchmarks, it can generate pages very slightly slower than real HN. (dang shared some timings on a particularly busy page, along with how many views it got over a certain time period, for benchmarking throughput. I never got around to verifying whether I can handle 24 million views a day, though, so I'd imagine something might break if you scale this up. On the other hand, I think it'll hold up.) If you're particularly offended that this is copying your comments, claim your account by going to your profile (for example, I would go to https://news.ycombinator.lol/user?id=sillysaurusx ) and then click "claim" at the bottom. It'll ask you to put a 6 digit code into your real HN profile, at which point you'll be able to reset your cloned profile's password. Log in, go to your profile page, and set "redact" to "yes", the same way you'd set "showdead" to "yes" on HN. So, why make this? Eh, call it an art project. That's code for "It would've been a lot funnier with AI generated comments, but I seem to have stopped working on this for now." I'll post an update someday, if I can figure out how to do it without paying hundreds of dollars of API token prices. /ask and /show are missing. Those were the only two features left to clone. But pretty much everything else is there. It's been running for a couple months now, so I suppose it's stable enough for a public showing. Not that there's any reason to look. Shoo! Go find a more worthy project to devote your attention to. :) Kind of melancholy admitting that I spent four months with only something pointless to show for it. But then again, here's the punchline: go to any random comment on HN, then in the url change .com to .lol and you'll see an almost pixel perfect recreation. For example, https://news.ycombinator.lol/item?id=49995615 Sadly you can't form a loop, because if you edit your original comment with a link to itself, you'd only be able to go from HN to .lol to HN. But you could list both and switch between them as much as you want. For example: https://news.ycombinator.lol/item?id=49996495 https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49996495 This project was one of the most technically demanding things I've ever done. People look at HN and go oh, that? That looks easy. If you think so, I invite you to write it yourself -- it's an exercise that'll certainly make you a better programmer, and gain appreciation for how many subtle features we enjoy here on HN. Ha, and I just discovered a new one. I mixed up the "title" and "url" boxes just now. HN popped up a nice looking overlay that said "please enter a URL", pointing to the actual url box. https://i.imgur.com/agFas7x.png The HN team is always adding something or anothe

Preferred (nice to have, not required) - Professional voice-over experience (dubbing/ADR, audiobook, podcasting) in a conversational rather than commercial/announcer register. - Baseline audio hygiene: comfortable setting mic distance and catching noise, clipping, or distortion yourself. - An existing home recording setup already treated for sound. Your Data & Privacy Before any session recording, you'll be asked to review and sign a Consent Form covering how your voice recordings are collected, used (including to train synthesized/AI voice models), shared with approved partners, retained, and how to exercise your data rights (access, correction, deletion, and more, depending on where you live). Our research tackles some of the hardest open problems in AI safety: assessing the alignment of frontier models, developing control protocols and monitoring methods, preserving the monitorability, understanding failure modes in multi-agent systems and recursive self-improvement. As a Research Scientist on this team, you will conduct research and build evaluations, tools, and datasets that help us understand and reduce risks from frontier AI systems. For example, you might do any or all of the following: Design and stress-test control protocols and monitoring systems that detect and limit unsafe behavior by AI models and agents in deployment; Build alignment evaluations that probe for deception, sabotage, scheming, reward hacking, and other misaligned behaviors; Study monitorability, including whether a model’s reasoning stays faithful and legible enough to supervise, and how training methods and deployment practices can preserve or erode it; Investigate risks that emerge when multiple AI agents interact, such as collusion, coordination failures and steerability; Develop threat models and evaluations for AI systems that automate AI research and development, to track progress toward recursive self-improvement and inform preparedness planning; Work with government agencies and other labs to scope and design evaluations that measure and mitigate risks from advanced AI; Publish research and evaluation methodologies, and write technical reports for policymakers. Ideally you’d have: Commitment to our mission of promoting safe, secure, and trustworthy AI as capabilities continue to advance. Practical experience conducting technical research collaboratively. Familiarity with current research in at least one of the areas above. A track record of published research in machine learning, particularly in AI safety and alignment. At least three years of experience working on sophisticated ML problems, in research or product development. leads.title: Show HN: Privatrak – no-code, privacy-first product analytics
leads.description: Hi HN! Quick story how it started: I was a freelance web developer in the past and also worked for several companies on web applications. For some projects we didn’t have analytics at all and we had to ask ourselves too many times what our users actually use in the product. Finding a good solution was painful, since we couldn’t use a consent banner (a lot of customers from the government) and existing tools were hard to set up so nobody took the time. I started with this idea already many years ago, but only really got to develop it in the past year. So what is Privatrak? A product tracking tool which is simple to set up and doesn’t require any code for most use cases. It can be used just by tagging elements on your site in the browser. From that, funnels and analytics dashboards can be created. I also wanted to make it as easy as possible to use with AI agents, hence there is a MCP server which can be used to question the data and set up the project (every change an AI agent makes is tracked and can also easily be undone). It doesn’t store any sensitive user data and can be used without a consent banner or cookies. Sessions are calculated based on a hash that consists of the users IP address + user agent + random rotating salt (IP address and user agent are never stored) and are aggregated for each day, so the data basically only points at a group of users in the end. In many cases this is fine. Often you are only curious about a specific feature or trends and not what a specific user did. If you need to track people over multiple days or need session replays, this is not the right tool. My main goal in posting here is to get some feedback for the product. Is the daily cutoff for sessions a dealbreaker for you? I just launched it and currently only have a handful of people actually using it. I built a demo project for everybody to see how it looks without having to sign up: https://demo.privatrak.com/

leads.title: AI Safety Residency - SLPreP
leads.description: Job Application for AI Safety Residency - SLPreP at Scale AI Back to jobs AI Safety Residency - SLPreP Canada; United Kingdom; United States Apply About the Program The Human Frontier Collective (HFC) brings researchers and scientists together to tackle consequential problems in AI. In partnership with Scale Labs Preparedness and Policy (SLPreP) , we are building a small cohort of researchers to work on the empirical foundations of AI safety. The work includes thinking about various failure modes, evaluating whether safety controls hold up under pressure in realistic settings, and studying how AI agents (mis-)behave over long-horizon tasks. Residents take open research questions like these and turn them into work that improves how frontier AI systems are evaluated and safeguarded. Research Areas Mentors will guide AI safety residents on projects in AI safety research areas, such as: AI control and chain-of-thought monitoring: Developing techniques to oversee and constrain AI systems, including monitoring their reasoning to detect harmful intent or deception. Alignment red-teaming: Developing science around testing whether models have hidden goals, misaligned behaviors or unsafe tendencies. Multi-agent safety: Studying the risks that emerge when multiple agents interact, such as collusion, coordinated failures, or unexpected collective behavior. Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) safety: Investigating how to keep AI systems safe and aligned as AIs increasingly contribute to their own development. Science of Evaluations: Examining when and how models recognize they're being tested, and how situational awareness affects the reliability/validity of evaluations. Misuse risks: Developing methods to assess how AI systems could be exploited by malicious actors, including evaluating their potential to enable harmful activities. Projects are matched to demonstrated expertise; we don’t expect any candidate to cover every area. leads.title: Show HN: What a major earthquake does to Vancouver
leads.description: About 10 years ago, I attended a presentation by someone who had compiled existing engineering reports to describe the impact of a major earthquake on infrastructure in British Columbia. It was really striking, and it has stayed in the back of my mind ever since. I am now the point of contact for downtown Vancouver in the French community's emergency network, and it drives me nuts that most people I talk to have no emergency kit at home and basically no water. People are shocked, or in denial, when I mention that it could take weeks to restore electricity and that they will have to rely on their own food and water for at least several days. So I decided to build a public-facing site that compiles existing information, as a way to lay out the facts and help convince people, instead of hearing back that "the army will come" or that "there are emergency food reserves" (there aren't). I see this as a citizen initiative, with one main message: go buy some water and canned food, it's your civic duty. I relied on AI agents to compile the information, which is spread across hundreds of reports. With different levels of validation, plus my own review, I am confident the information is reliable, even if some details may not be fully up to date. The process took 2–3 weeks, alongside work, a toddler and a baby! I'm posting it here because: 1) I'm curious to get feedback and suggestions. 2) Many HN readers are on the West Coast or in other seismic areas, so even if you're not in Vancouver, the general recommendations may be of interest. Be smart: buy some food and water. Cheers Thomas
